slides.title: Conformal Operators
slides.notes: Open by naming the shift in Chapter 16: the conformal model is no longer just a catalog of points, spheres, lines, and circles. It becomes an operator calculus. The visible source span marker records the assigned manifest boundary, while the lecture content follows the executable chapter notebook and its original diagnostics.

slides.title: Operator Grammar
slides.notes: Frame every transformation as a sandwich action. A versor or rotor is valuable because it applies to points, circles, lines, spheres, and blades by the same grammatical rule. Students should see covariance as the main promise: construct first or transform first, and the object family still fits together.

slides.title: Conformal Point Bookkeeping
slides.notes: Review the minimal bookkeeping before naming the operators. A finite point is lifted to a null representative by adding the two null coordinates, and Euclidean distance is recovered from the conformal inner product. This slide supplies the invariant ledger that later checks translations, rotations, and dilations.

slides.title: Translators Fix Infinity
slides.notes: Treat translation as the least surprising conformal operator and use it to set the standard. The translator moves every finite point by the same vector while leaving the infinity direction fixed. The visual grid shift is deliberately simple so the algebraic invariant, not the drawing, carries the force.

slides.title: Rotors And Motors
slides.notes: Connect Euclidean rotors to motors by composing rotation and translation. The point samples move, but the circle remains a circle and the oriented line remains a line because the sandwich action is covariant. Emphasize that a motor is not merely a point transform; it transports whole geometric objects.

slides.title: Dilations Are Null-Plane Boosts
slides.notes: Present uniform scaling as a conformal operation rather than an affine afterthought. In the embedded point, the null coordinates trade weight, and finite coordinates appear scaled only after normalization. This is why the dilation has a clean exponential form in the plane spanned by the two null directions.

slides.title: Order Locates The Center
slides.notes: Use the noncommuting triangle paths as a concrete debugging test. Translating and then scaling is not the same as scaling and then translating because the translation vector is itself scaled in one order. The difference vector tells students where the dilation center has effectively moved.

slides.title: Inversion Is Sphere Reflection
slides.notes: Name inversion as reflection in a sphere and make the local conformal claim precise. Points move radially by reciprocal distance, the mirror circle is fixed, and applying the operation twice returns the original sample. The line-to-circle image prepares students for round objects changing visible type.

slides.title: Sandwich Actions Preserve Round Families
slides.notes: Slow down on object covariance. A line may become a circle after inversion, but it stays inside the extended family of round objects. The same sandwich action transports the object representation, so incidence and angle checks remain meaningful even when the Euclidean category label changes.

slides.title: Transversions Bend The Grid
slides.notes: Define a transversion as inversion, translation, and inversion again. It looks nonlinear in the plane because infinity is no longer held fixed, yet it is still conformal away from the pole. Ask students to identify the inverse check: changing the parameter sign brings ordinary samples back.

slides.title: Similarity Orbits And Motors
slides.notes: Move from one-shot actions to repeated actions. Combining a translator, rotor, and dilation gives a similarity motor whose orbit can generate shell-like trails of circles. The important invariant is not the artistic spiral; it is the repeated circle-fit residual that stays small at every iteration.

slides.title: Loxodromes From Rotor Plus Dilation
slides.notes: Use the loxodrome to show why conformal operators are useful for motion, not only construction. A logarithmic spiral in the plane meets radial rays at a constant angle, and stereographic projection preserves that angle. On the sphere, the result is a constant-bearing curve rather than a great circle.

slides.title: Changing Infinity Changes Geometry
slides.notes: This is the conceptual wide angle. The conformal machinery does not force Euclidean infinity to be the only preserved object. Preserving a real unit sphere gives the hyperbolic disk picture, while the spherical reading turns planar circles into projected great circles with antipodal boundary behavior.

slides.title: Invariant Check Panel
slides.notes: Make the diagnostics explicit and reusable. The notebook checks nullness, metric preservation, involution of inversion, round-object preservation, transversion inverse behavior, loxodrome bearing stability, and torus orbit residuals. These are not decorative numbers; they are the regression tests for the geometric claims.

slides.title: Worked Debugging Exercise
slides.notes: Ask students to debug an operator product by predicting both the visual behavior and the invariant ledger before computing. The exercise separates three questions: what finite points do, what infinity does, and what object family is preserved. This mirrors the practical workflow in a conformal geometry codebase.

slides.title: Chapter Synthesis
slides.notes: Close by tying the operator names back to the same rule. Translators, rotors, motors, dilations, inversions, and transversions are different factors in one conformal grammar. The main takeaway is that geometric algebra lets software apply the same sandwich action to points, objects, and transformation products.
